title: My Mom Tried to Sabotage My Birthday Party... Again

segments.x: I just turned 50. And uh my friends threw me a party. My friend Julia threw me and my soul sister, my bro, Ali Wong, have uh matching birthdays. But between the flying mahjong chips, the mushroom tea, and the ear-popping USC marching band, there was a moment when my [music] parents, who are in

their 80s, my dad had a stroke 7 years ago, so he's in a wheelchair, they arrived to the party. >> [music] >> You know, my mom, you know, I'm her baby boy. She's like, "My baby boy's turning 50. Let me make some mandu. Let me make some tofu. Let me make some kimbap. Let

me make some kimchi jjigae." I go, "Mom, I told my mom no." I said, "No. Meow. No is a complete sentence. That's called a boundary." It's like, "I need to do a hey. The whole party's catered. Just show up, have a good time. My friends are throwing a huge party for me. Just

show up and have fun. You don't need to make anything. You don't need to bring anything." If you guys want to know where I come from, a little insight into who I am, you know, she's bringing me my hanbok, a traditional Korean wear. She wants me to wear all that stuff.

>> [music] >> The night before I get a video, she sends a video to the family group chat. It's her at five [music] frying pans going, cooking stuff. She's like, "Haha, look at me." Editor, I'll send you the video. This is a metaphor for like our whole relationship, our whole life together. She gets out of the Uber and

she drops the trays of mandu. Broken glass everywhere. And what does she do? She runs inside, gets some paper plate, and starts trying to save dumplings that have glass [music] in it. She's like brushing the glass off. I go, "What the [—] are you doing, Mom? No one's eating glass dumplings. That's done." I told my mom, "No. Do not do

that." And then she brings the rest of the food in, and I told her, there was delicious food, but you know, chicken wings, unless you eat them straight off the fryer right after they're cooked, they get cold pretty quick. She shows up to the party and she has trays and trays of Korean food. Dumplings, kimchi

pancakes, everything. And so people at the party ended [music] up liking my mom's food better than the catered food. And then in the end she goes, "See? I was right." Told my sister-in-law, "Man, this food's pretty good." And she goes, "Oh, she didn't make any of it." I go, "What?" "Yeah, she just filmed

herself making it for 2 seconds and then her assistant made it." >> [laughter] >> Lies upon lies upon lies. There's some truth in there somewhere. She did cook it for 2 seconds. And that's why I say I tell lies [music] to tell the truth.
>> That's great. >> Yeah, that that's a great >> I'm on baby. >> Okay, thank you. >> [music]

editorial.summary: A 2:42 birthday-party story whose uploader title calls the mother’s behavior sabotage, while the transcript is more layered. An unresolved storyteller turns fifty; friends including spoken references to Julia and Ali Wong organize a party with mahjong chips, mushroom tea and a USC marching band. Parents in their eighties arrive; the father reportedly had a stroke seven years earlier and uses a wheelchair. The speaker performs his mother offering Korean foods and a hanbok despite an explicit no/boundary. She films herself cooking for the family chat, drops mandu amid broken glass and tries to salvage dumplings; he rejects contaminated food. Guests reportedly prefer her food, then a sister-in-law says an assistant actually made it. The speaker concludes “lies upon lies,” some truth, and “I tell lies to tell the truth.” Every care, conflict, hazard, hidden-labor and storytelling idea remains. Sabotage intent, private identities, medical details, guest consensus, assistant credit/employment and line-level voices remain unverified.
